title: Five companions
hookLine: Kondañña and four others join him in the forest near Uruvela
last: TWO TEACHERS — GOOD, BUT NOT THE END.

cards: If you've ever swum laps at six in the morning, you know the regulars. The man in the blue cap. The woman who always takes the far lane.
You've never learned their names, and you'd never call them friends. But on a cold morning you think of them, already in the water, and you go. The wanderer has left both teachers.

He walks on through the kingdom of Magadha to a place near the village of Uruvela: a pleasant grove, a clear river with good banks, villages nearby for alms. This, he thinks, is a good place to strive.
And he isn't alone for long.

teach.b: Five wanderers join him: Kondañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama and Assaji.

teach.h: KONDAÑÑA SAID IT AT THE NAMING.
teach.b: The later telling gives Kondañña a remarkable backstory. Remember the naming day, when the brahmins read the marks on the baby prince? Most of them said: a great king or a great teacher.
The youngest said only one thing: this child will become a Buddha. That youngest brahmin was Kondañña. Years later, hearing that the prince has gone forth, he comes to find him, bringing four others.
Why would five serious seekers attach themselves to this one? Because, the story says, they could see what he was: someone who wouldn't stop.
They serve him, sweep, bring water, and wait. When he finds the answer, they say, he'll tell us. Hold on to these five.
They'll walk away from him in anger, and they'll come back. They'll be the first people who ever hear him teach. But that's weeks away.
For now, the story shows something simple. Even this search, often told as one man's lonely quest, had company.
Buddhism later names three treasures, and one of them is the sangha, the community of practice.
Before there was a Buddha or a teaching, there was already something like a sangha: six men in a forest, keeping each other going.

how: Buddhists take refuge in the three jewels, the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, and many practice with a community, meditating together because company makes the practice easier to keep.

games.q: who's in the forest — tap the pairs.

s: the wanderer spent his whole search completely alone
five companions joined him near Uruvela.
in the later telling, Kondañña was at the prince's naming day
the youngest brahmin, who said he would become a Buddha.
they were fellow seekers who served him, waiting for him to find the way.

games.q: you're Kondañña. years ago you said this child would become a Buddha. now you hear he's gone forth. what do you do?
o: stay home: prophecies are just words.
find him, and bring four others.
send a letter wishing him well.
games.why: in the telling, Kondañña goes looking for him with four companions, and the five join him in the forest.

practice: Right now, somewhere, people you'll never meet are doing what you're doing: a nun in Sri Lanka settling onto her mat, a nurse taking one slow breath in a hospital stairwell, someone on a bus with their eyes closed, counting.

On each of five breaths, picture one of them, five strangers on the same road, the way the five found the wanderer. Then let them go and sit with your own breath, knowing it isn't the only one being watched.

wordCard.voice: Five companions. Kondañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama and Assaji: the wanderers who joined him near Uruvela, waiting for him to find the way.

orig.note: Pali: the group of five, the name Buddhists give these five companions.

carryVoice: Your line: you don't go alone. Even when it feels like you do. Day forty-three, and a new week begun.
